chapter_summary:
A robot that knows where it is but has no map is lost in the dark. A robot that has a map but does not know where it is on the map is equally lost. **SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping)** is the problem of building a map of an unknown environment while simultaneously keeping track of the robot's location within that map. SLAM is one of the most important and challenging problems in robotics, and it is the enabling technology for autonomous navigation in unknown environments.

Before tackling SLAM, we first understand **mapping** — the problem of building a map given known robot poses. The most common map representation in robotics is the **occupancy grid map**. An occupancy grid divides the environment into a grid of cells, and each cell stores the probability that it is occupied by an obstacle. A cell with probability 0.9 is almost certainly occupied. A cell with probability 0.1 is almost certainly free. A cell with probability 0.5 is unknown.

The occupancy grid is updated using a **Bayesian filtering** approach. When the robot receives a sensor measurement (e.g., from a LiDAR or sonar), we update the occupancy probability of each cell using the **inverse sensor model**. The inverse sensor model tells us the probability that a cell is occupied given the sensor measurement and the robot's pose.

For a range sensor like LiDAR, the inverse sensor model works as follows:
- Cells along the ray up to the measured distance are likely free (the sensor would have detected an obstacle if one were there).
- The cell at the measured distance is likely occupied (the sensor detected something there).
- Cells beyond the measured distance are unknown (the sensor did not see them).

The update is done using the log-odds representation to avoid numerical underflow:

```
l_t = l_{t-1} + inverse_sensor_model - l_0
```

Where `l_t` is the log-odds of occupancy at time `t`, and `l_0` is the prior log-odds (typically 0, corresponding to probability 0.5).

```matlab
function grid = occupancy_grid_mapping(grid, pose, range_reading, angles, cell_size)
    % pose: [x, y, theta]
    % range_reading: distances from LiDAR
    % angles: angles of each LiDAR beam
    
    for i = 1:length(range_reading)
        % End point of the ray
        x_end = pose(1) + range_reading(i) * cos(pose(3) + angles(i));
        y_end = pose(2) + range_reading(i) * sin(pose(3) + angles(i));
        
        % Ray tracing: mark cells along the ray as free
        [x_cells, y_cells] = bresenham_line(pose(1), pose(2), x_end, y_end);
        for j = 1:length(x_cells)-1
            grid(y_cells(j), x_cells(j)) = grid(y_cells(j), x_cells(j)) - 0.1;
        end
        
        % Mark the end cell as occupied
        grid(y_cells(end), x_cells(end)) = grid(y_cells(end), x_cells(end)) + 0.4;
    end
end
```

**SLAM** combines mapping with localization. The challenge is that the robot's pose is unknown, so we cannot simply map as described above. The error in the robot's pose estimate (from odometry) causes the map to become inconsistent. Small errors accumulate over time, and the map becomes distorted.

There are two main formulations of SLAM:
- **Online SLAM:** Estimate the current robot pose and the map, given all measurements up to the current time. This is what a robot needs to navigate in real-time.
- **Full SLAM:** Estimate the entire robot trajectory and the map, given all measurements. This is used for offline map refinement and loop closure.

The SLAM problem can be formulated as a probabilistic inference problem:

```
P(x_{0:t}, m | z_{1:t}, u_{1:t})
```

Where `x_{0:t}` is the robot trajectory, `m` is the map, `z_{1:t}` are the measurements, and `u_{1:t}` are the control inputs. This is a high-dimensional joint distribution, and computing it exactly is intractable. SLAM algorithms approximate this distribution using various techniques:

- **EKF-SLAM:** Uses the Extended Kalman Filter to estimate the joint state of the robot pose and landmark positions. Scales poorly to large environments (the covariance matrix grows with the number of landmarks).
- **FastSLAM:** Uses particle filters to represent the pose distribution and EKFs for each landmark. More scalable than EKF-SLAM.
- **Graph-based SLAM:** Represents the SLAM problem as a graph where nodes are robot poses and landmarks, and edges are constraints from measurements. The graph is optimized using nonlinear least-squares (e.g., the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm). This is the dominant approach in modern SLAM (e.g., Google Cartographer, g2o, GTSAM).
- **Visual SLAM:** Uses cameras as the primary sensor. Examples include ORB-SLAM, LSD-SLAM, and SVO. These systems extract features from images, estimate camera motion, and build sparse or dense maps.

**Loop closure** is a critical concept in SLAM. When the robot returns to a previously visited location, it should recognize that it has been there before and correct the accumulated drift. Loop closure detection is typically done by comparing the current sensor data (image or LiDAR scan) to all previous data and finding a match. Once a loop is detected, the graph optimization algorithm adjusts the entire trajectory to be consistent with the loop closure constraint.

```matlab
% Simple loop closure detection using image similarity
% Compare current image descriptor to all previous descriptors
similarities = cosine_similarity(current_descriptor, all_descriptors);
[best_match, best_idx] = max(similarities);
if best_match > threshold
    disp('Loop closure detected!');
    % Add loop closure constraint to graph
    add_loop_closure_edge(graph, current_pose_idx, best_idx);
end
```

screens.title: Occupancy Grid Mapping and SLAM
screens.subtitle: Build maps from sensor rays, manage uncertainty, and solve localization while mapping

narration.text: We begin with two tightly linked challenges in mobile robotics: mapping the world and knowing where you are inside it. In this lesson you will learn how occupancy grid maps represent space as per-cell probabilities, how range sensors produce evidence for free and occupied cells through the inverse sensor model, and why log-odds updates keep those probabilities numerically stable. Then we expand to SLAM — simultaneous localization and mapping — where pose uncertainty and mapping are solved together, not independently. You'll see the practical contrast between online SLAM, which estimates the current pose for real-time navigation, and full SLAM, which refines an entire trajectory using all measurements for offline accuracy. We will also review algorithm families you will encounter in practice: EKF approaches, particle-based FastSLAM, and graph-based optimization methods. A concrete MATLAB mapping example is included, so you can implement an occupancy grid and watch LiDAR rays carve free space while endpoints mark obstacles. By the end, you should understand the core trade-offs: accuracy versus computational cost, incremental updates versus global refinement, and how loop closure corrects drift. Reflect on this: when mapping a featureless corridor, which part of SLAM becomes hardest — perception, association, or optimization?

keyIdea.text: Occupancy grids convert range data into per-cell probabilities using an inverse sensor model and log-odds; SLAM couples pose estimation with mapping so each problem helps correct the other.

screens.title: Occupancy Grid Map
screens.subtitle: Cells hold probabilities that describe free, occupied, or unknown space

narration.text: An occupancy grid divides the environment into a regular 2D grid where each cell stores the probability it is occupied. This is a discrete, cell-wise representation that turns raw sensor measurements into a spatial belief useful for path planning and collision avoidance. A probability near 0.9 means the cell is almost certainly occupied, 0.1 means almost certainly free, and 0.5 means unknown. The grid abstracts geometry into a format robots can reason about efficiently. A common misunderstanding is to treat each cell as an absolute truth; instead, cells represent belief and must be updated incrementally as new sensor readings arrive. For example, a LiDAR ray that passes through several cells without returning indicates the cells along the ray are more likely free; the ray endpoint suggests occupancy at that location. Practically, this lets a robot fuse many partial views into a coherent map: as you drive around a rectangular obstacle and sweep LiDAR, the central obstacle cells accumulate higher occupancy probability while surrounding cells become more confidently free. Key takeaway: occupancy grids trade continuous geometry for a structured probabilistic map that is simple to update and integrate with planning.

keyIdea.title: Occupancy grid
keyIdea.text: A grid of per-cell occupancy probabilities: a probabilistic map useful for navigation and sensor fusion.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Occupancy Grid Map
Definition

Cell-based probability map

Each grid cell stores P(occupied). Cells start as unknown (0.5) and are updated as the robot observes the world. The representation is compact, supports incremental updates, and integrates naturally with planning.

Example
A LiDAR ray that sees an obstacle at 3 m will make cells before 3 m more likely free and the cell at 3 m more likely occupied.
Common mistake
Treating probabilities as binary. Occupancy is belief, so keep fusing evidence instead of hard-thresholding too early.
Key Takeaway

Occupancy grids let a robot accumulate uncertain sensor evidence into a usable map for navigation.

Visual intuition
0.9
occupied
0.5
unknown
0.1
free
Analogy
Think of the grid as an image built over time: each scan paints brush strokes of certainty until the picture of the environment becomes clear.

screens.title: Inverse Sensor Model
screens.subtitle: How a range reading updates cell occupancy beliefs

narration.text: The inverse sensor model answers a specific question: given a sensor measurement and the robot pose, what is the probability that a particular cell is occupied? For a range sensor like LiDAR the model is intuitive. Cells along the ray before the measured distance are likely free because the sensor would have returned an earlier hit if they were obstacles. The cell at the measured distance is likely occupied because a return occurred there. Cells beyond the measured distance are left unknown because the sensor did not observe them. Implementations often encode this as fixed likelihood values: a free-likelihood for traversed cells and an occupied-likelihood for the endpoint. A useful implementation detail is to convert probabilities into log-odds so that successive measurements add linearly. A misconception is to update only the endpoint and ignore the free evidence along the ray; neglecting free updates leaves large swaths of unknown or wrongly-occupied cells and harms planning. Example: a single 180° LiDAR sweep at 1° resolution will produce 180 rays. For each ray, mark intermediate cells with a free update and the endpoint with an occupied update, then fuse these updates into the grid. The takeaway: inverse sensor models provide the rulebook for turning raw readings into evidence distributed across multiple cells.

keyIdea.title: Inverse sensor model
keyIdea.text: Maps a range reading into per-cell evidence: free along the ray, occupied at the endpoint, unknown beyond.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Inverse Sensor Model
Process

Ray → cells → updates

Step 1
For each LiDAR beam, compute the ray endpoint in world coordinates using robot pose and beam angle.
Step 2
Trace the ray through grid cells (e.g., Bresenham) and apply a free update to traversed cells.
Step 3
Apply an occupied update to the endpoint cell and leave cells beyond unknown.
Common mistake
Do not ignore free updates. If you only mark endpoints, free space remains unknown and planning can be overly conservative.
Concrete example
180° LiDAR, 1° steps
For each of 180 beams, compute endpoint, run Bresenham to get cells along the beam, decrement log-odds slightly for traversed cells and increment more for the endpoint cell. Repeat across poses to build the map.
Key Takeaway

Distribute sensor evidence: free evidence along rays is as important as endpoints for a correct map.

screens.title: Log-Odds Representation
screens.subtitle: Why log-odds make repeated updates simple and stable

narration.text: When fusing many sensor readings into a per-cell probability, repeated multiplication of probabilities can cause numerical instability. The log-odds representation converts probabilities to a log-odds value l = log(p / (1 - p)), and updates become additive. The typical recursive rule is l_t = l_{t-1} + inverse_sensor_model - l_0, where l_0 is the prior log-odds (usually zero for a 0.5 prior). Using log-odds prevents underflow when fusing many weak measurements and simplifies incremental updates because you add evidence instead of multiplying likelihoods. A practical example: if the sensor gives a modest occupied-likelihood each time you hit the same cell, repeated occupied observations increase l linearly, and converting back to probability gives a clear sense of growing confidence. A common misconception is to confuse log-odds updates with arbitrary offsets; the inverse sensor model provides the correct evidence terms to add. Takeaway: use log-odds to keep updates numerically robust and conceptually additive so each new beam contributes directly to belief. Log-Odds Representation means convert probabilities to log-odds for additive, numerically-stable updates when fusing repeated sensor evidence.. In practical terms, why log-odds make repeated updates simple and stable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Log-odds
keyIdea.text: Convert probabilities to log-odds for additive, numerically-stable updates when fusing repeated sensor evidence.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Log-Odds Representation
Why use it?

Additive updates and numerical stability

Log-odds turn multiplication of small probabilities into addition of evidence terms. This prevents underflow and makes incremental fusion straightforward.

Update rule
l_t = l_{t-1} + inverse_sensor_model - l_0. With l_0 = 0 for a 0.5 prior, you simply add sensor evidence to the existing log-odds.
Concrete example
Repeated hits
If each occupied observation contributes +0.4 in log-odds, three consistent hits raise l by +1.2, and converting back to probability yields a high occupancy belief. This additive behavior is simple to reason about.
Key Takeaway

Use log-odds for safe, additive fusion of sensor evidence and to avoid numerical underflow from repeated multiplications.

screens.title: Ray Tracing and Bresenham
screens.subtitle: Efficiently enumerate cells along a sensor ray

narration.text: To apply free updates along a beam you must find which grid cells the beam crosses. Bresenham's line algorithm is a classic solution: it efficiently computes the integer grid cells approximating a straight line between two coordinates. In occupancy mapping, we use Bresenham to list every cell from the robot's cell to the endpoint cell. Each traversed cell gets a free update, and the final cell gets an occupied update. A practical concern is discretization: the robot pose and endpoint coordinates must be converted to grid indices using the cell size. Another subtlety is handling sensor range limits: if the range reading is beyond the sensor max, treat cells up to the max as free and avoid marking an endpoint occupied. A common misconception is to apply free updates only to a small neighborhood around the beam; doing so leaves thin gaps and reduces map fidelity. Example: for a 10 m × 10 m world with a 100×100 grid, cell_size = 0.1 m; converting a 3.2 m endpoint to indices ensures Bresenham enumerates exactly the cells to mark. Takeaway: robust ray tracing is crucial for correct free-space evidence and good maps.

keyIdea.title: Ray tracing
keyIdea.text: Use Bresenham or equivalent to enumerate cells along a beam so free evidence is applied correctly to traversed cells.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Ray Tracing
Algorithm

Bresenham for occupancy grids

Convert world coordinates to grid indices using cell size, then run Bresenham to list cells on the ray. Each listed cell except the last receives a free update; the last receives an occupied update if within sensor range.

Note
If the reading equals the sensor max or is invalid, apply only free updates and do not mark an endpoint occupied.
Concrete scenario
100×100 grid, 10 m world
With cell_size = 0.1 m, a 3.2 m endpoint maps to index floor(3.2 / 0.1) = 32. Bresenham enumerates cells from the robot cell to index 32 so you can apply free and occupied updates consistently.
Key Takeaway

Precise cell indexing and ray tracing ensure free-space evidence is applied correctly, which is essential for accurate maps.

screens.title: Occupancy Grid Mapping — MATLAB Example
screens.subtitle: A script that casts rays, updates log-odds, and visualizes the grid

narration.text: Let's walk through the provided MATLAB-style mapping function in concrete terms. The function accepts a grid, the robot pose, range_readings, beam angles, and cell_size. For each range reading it computes the ray endpoint using pose and beam angle, then runs a ray tracer such as Bresenham to get the sequence of grid indices from the robot to the endpoint. Traversed cells receive a small negative log-odds change to reduce occupancy belief (free evidence), while the final cell receives a positive increment to increase occupancy belief. Doing this for every beam and for each robot pose you visit results in an evolving log-odds grid. A common pitfall is to forget coordinate rounding rules when indexing the grid, which can shift the map. Another is to incorrectly apply free updates to the endpoint cell or to apply occupied updates when the range is invalid or beyond the sensor max. Example: the script example subtracts 0.1 from traversed cells and adds 0.4 to the endpoint. Those numeric values are tunable and reflect sensor confidence; test them in simulation. The takeaway: the implementation directly follows the inverse sensor model and log-odds principles and is a great starting point for hands-on mapping.

keyIdea.title: MATLAB mapping
keyIdea.text: Loop over beams: compute endpoint, trace cells, decrement log-odds for free cells, increment for endpoint, repeat across poses.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › MATLAB Example
Code snippet
function grid = occupancy_grid_mapping(grid, pose, range_reading, angles, cell_size)
    % pose: [x, y, theta]
    % range_reading: distances from LiDAR
    % angles: angles of each LiDAR beam

    for i = 1:length(range_reading)
        % End point of the ray
        x_end = pose(1) + range_reading(i) * cos(pose(3) + angles(i));
        y_end = pose(2) + range_reading(i) * sin(pose(3) + angles(i));

        % Ray tracing: mark cells along the ray as free
        [x_cells, y_cells] = bresenham_line(pose(1), pose(2), x_end, y_end);
        for j = 1:length(x_cells)-1
            grid(y_cells(j), x_cells(j)) = grid(y_cells(j), x_cells(j)) - 0.1;
        end

        % Mark the end cell as occupied
        grid(y_cells(end), x_cells(end)) = grid(y_cells(end), x_cells(end)) + 0.4;
    end
end
Explanation
  • Compute world endpoint from pose and beam angle to locate the detected obstacle.
  • Use an integer ray tracer to enumerate intervening cells and apply a free update.
  • Apply an occupied update to the final cell if the reading is valid.
Practical tips
Tune the free and occupied increments to match sensor noise. Convert probabilities to log-odds externally if you prefer additive updates.

screens.title: Mapping vs SLAM
screens.subtitle: Why mapping with known poses is easier than SLAM

narration.text: Mapping with known poses assumes the robot's position at each measurement is given and correct. Under that assumption you project sensor returns into the map directly and accumulate occupancy updates. SLAM removes that luxury: the robot must estimate its own pose from noisy odometry and sensors while simultaneously building the map. The coupling creates a two-way dependency: pose errors distort the map, and map errors can lead to incorrect pose estimates. A common way to think about this is a chicken-and-egg problem where solving one requires good knowledge of the other. Online SLAM focuses on estimating only the current pose and the map for immediate navigation, which keeps computation bounded. Full SLAM estimates the entire trajectory and the map using all data for global consistency, which is more computationally demanding but yields better final maps and enables loop closure to correct drift. Example: if odometry drifts slowly over a long loop, an online-only system will accrue an increasingly warped map; full SLAM with loop closure can detect the loop and globally adjust the trajectory and map. Takeaway: SLAM is fundamentally harder because two coupled estimates must be solved together rather than independently.

keyIdea.title: Mapping vs SLAM
keyIdea.text: Known-pose mapping projects measurements into the grid directly; SLAM must estimate poses and the map jointly, which couples errors and increases complexity.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Mapping vs SLAM
Mapping (known poses)
Direct projection
With accurate poses, sensor readings are transformed into world coordinates and directly used to update the occupancy grid. There's no need to infer pose from the same sensors used for mapping.
Example: a robot with motion capture or a precise GPS can focus only on mapping, producing consistent maps quickly.
SLAM (unknown poses)
Coupled estimation
Pose uncertainty and map uncertainty are entangled. Errors in pose estimates distort the map, and bad maps can mislead pose estimation. Solving SLAM requires techniques that jointly reason about both.
Example: odometry drift over a long loop will warp a map unless loop closure and global optimization correct the trajectory.
Contrast
Online vs Full SLAM
Online SLAM estimates the current pose for navigation; full SLAM optimizes the whole trajectory offline for better global consistency.
Key Takeaway
Why SLAM is harder
Because pose and map must be estimated together, small errors amplify without global constraints like loop closure.

narration.text: There are multiple ways to approximate the intractable joint SLAM posterior. EKF-SLAM augments the robot pose and landmark positions into one Gaussian state with a covariance that captures uncertainty and correlations. It works for small environments but scales poorly because the covariance grows with landmarks. FastSLAM splits the problem: particles represent pose uncertainty while each particle maintains independent landmark estimates via small EKFs. This makes FastSLAM more scalable in many settings. Graph-based SLAM instead creates a graph where nodes are poses (and optionally landmarks) and edges encode constraints from odometry and observations; offline optimization minimizes a nonlinear least-squares objective to find a trajectory and map consistent with all measurements. This graph view is dominant in modern SLAM because it handles large-scale problems and loop closures naturally via constraint addition. Visual SLAM specializes to cameras and extracts image features to form constraints analogous to landmarks. A typical misconception is to think one family is strictly superior; in practice, the choice depends on sensor types, required scale, and computation. Takeaway: EKF is simple, FastSLAM adds scalability via particles, and graph-based methods are preferred for large, real-world systems because of efficient sparse optimization.

keyIdea.title: SLAM families
keyIdea.text: EKF, particle-based FastSLAM, and graph-based optimization are different trade-offs in accuracy, scalability, and computational cost.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › SLAM Families
EKF-SLAM
Joint Gaussian state
State and covariance include poses and landmarks. Updates use linearized Kalman math. Scales poorly as landmarks increase.
FastSLAM
Particles + per-landmark EKFs
Particles represent pose uncertainty while independent landmark filters keep per-particle map estimates. More scalable in many scenarios.
Graph-based
Constraint optimization
Nodes are poses/landmarks, edges are constraints. Nonlinear least-squares optimizes the whole graph and handles loop closures directly.
Practical note
Choose algorithms based on scale and sensor modality. Visual SLAM methods adapt these ideas to cameras, extracting features and building constraints from images instead of range endpoints.

screens.title: Loop Closure and Drift Correction
screens.subtitle: Recognizing places and tightening the map

narration.text: Loop closure is the process of recognizing that the robot has returned to a previously visited location and using that recognition to constrain and correct the map and trajectory. Drift from odometry and incremental errors will warp the map over long trajectories. Detecting a loop provides a strong constraint: the current pose must be consistent with an earlier pose and the observations between them. Typical loop closure detection methods compare current sensor descriptors to stored descriptors from past poses and declare a match when similarity is high. Once a loop is suggested, the system adds a constraint to the SLAM graph and runs a global optimization to tighten the whole trajectory. A simple example uses image descriptors and cosine similarity: if the current descriptor matches a previous one above a threshold, add a loop edge and optimize. Misconceptions include trusting a single, weak match; robust loop closure often requires geometric verification. Takeaway: loop closure is the mechanism that turns local incremental mapping into globally consistent maps by providing corrective constraints when revisiting places. Loop Closure and Drift Correction means detect revisits, add constraints, and optimize the graph to remove accumulated drift and restore global consistency.. In practical terms, recognizing places and tightening the map. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Loop closure
keyIdea.text: Detect revisits, add constraints, and optimize the graph to remove accumulated drift and restore global consistency.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Loop Closure
What it does
Correct accumulated drift
When a revisit is detected, add a constraint between the current and past poses. Then run global optimization to adjust the entire trajectory and the map.
Detection tip
Use descriptor similarity plus geometric verification to avoid false positives that could corrupt the map.
Simple loop detector
Descriptor matching
Compute similarities between the current descriptor and all previous descriptors, take the highest match, and check against a threshold. If it exceeds the threshold, declare a loop and add the constraint.
Key Takeaway

Loop closure provides the global constraints needed to correct drift and produce a consistent final map.

screens.title: Graph-Based SLAM
screens.subtitle: Representing poses and constraints as a graph for global optimization

narration.text: Graph-based SLAM models the estimation problem as a graph: nodes represent robot poses (and optionally landmarks), and edges represent constraints from odometry or observations. Each edge encodes a relative measurement and an associated uncertainty. The SLAM problem becomes an optimization: find node states that best satisfy all constraints in a nonlinear least-squares sense. When a loop closure is added, it becomes another edge that pulls the trajectory toward consistency with previous observations. The power of this approach lies in sparsity: typical graphs are sparse and can be optimized efficiently using specialized solvers. A common misconception is to think graph-based SLAM is only offline; while many systems perform full optimization offline, incremental solvers allow near-online operation by optimizing only affected parts of the graph. Example: add odometry edges along motion and observation edges when a landmark or scan match is found; when loop closure appears add the loop edge and re-optimize. Takeaway: graph-based SLAM turns SLAM into a constrained optimization problem where loop closures act as corrective anchors across the trajectory. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Avoid pitfalls in mapping and SLAM

narration.text: Before you run code or deploy a mapping system, be aware of common mistakes that frequently undermine results. First, incorrect coordinate transforms or integer rounding when converting world coordinates to grid indices will systematically shift the map. Always carefully check your world-to-grid math and test with a known point. Second, ignoring free-space updates along rays leaves large unknown regions and slows map convergence; apply both free and occupied updates. Third, treating probabilities as hard labels too early removes the ability to recover from false observations; keep continuous beliefs and threshold only for display. Fourth, poor loop-closure verification can introduce false constraints that corrupt the map: combine descriptor similarity with geometric checks before adding loop edges. Finally, tune log-odds increments to reflect sensor characteristics: very large increments can overconfidently lock incorrect beliefs, very small increments slow convergence. Example: in the MATLAB snippet the values -0.1 and +0.4 are reasonable starting points; validate them in simulation. Takeaway: careful coordinate handling, balanced evidence updates, and robust loop closure make mapping and SLAM reliable in practice. screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three core ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the three central ideas you should carry forward. First, an occupancy grid represents the world as per-cell probabilities and is updated by distributing sensor evidence along rays: free cells along the beam, occupied at the measured endpoint, and unknown beyond. Second, the log-odds representation makes repeated updates additive and numerically robust, which is important when fusing many scans over time. Third, SLAM couples mapping and localization: online SLAM supports live navigation by estimating the current pose and map, while full SLAM refines the entire trajectory offline using loop closures and global optimization. Remember the practical trade-offs: EKF-SLAM is conceptually simple but scales poorly, FastSLAM uses particles to capture pose uncertainty, and graph-based SLAM frames the problem as sparse optimization that naturally handles loop closure.
